articles.title: How a Hisense MiniLED TV can upgrade your living room
articles.description: TVs have come a long way in the last few years. MiniLED sets are slimmer, brighter, boast impressive features and also have the ability to double as monitors for all your gaming needs. If you’re looking for a new TV that can fit in with all the demands of modern life then MiniLED is the way to go. But, not all work in the same way though, so you’ll want one that gives the best performance in a wide range of settings and with a variety of content. Here’s some things to consider when deciding on a new TV that will fit your home. How will the TV cope in brightly lit rooms? Hisense The physical positioning of a TV can be tricky, as you’ll want to avoid strong sources of light from hitting the screen, say from a window, but also want the freedom to place it wherever best suits the size and shape of the room. A washed out screen due to reflections and poor brightness can seriously compromise your enjoyment of shows and movies, that’s why you’ll want a TV that can handle these kind of environments. The Hisense U6SF is a good choice and makes this scenario a whole lot easier thanks to its anti-reflection and glare-free technology. These work to preserve shadow detail and color accuracy all while reducing reflections and surface glare from the sun or other forms of lighting. This means you can fit the TV into your room, rather than arranging the room around the TV, all in the knowledge that it will provide a consistent and clear picture. Another reason you can be confident of excellent visual performance from the Hisense U6SF is its Hi-QLED MiniLED technology. This includes the PowerFocus lens system, which employs single-refraction lenses to guide light accurately to where it needs to be on the screen. Unlike some other MiniLED TVs, this allows the U6SF to precisely focus the brightness and contrast to 160 local dimming zones, which results in deeper blacks, luminous highlights, sharper edges and a more immersive viewing experience. Movies and TVs shows look distinct and balanced, plus any content will be rendered with pin-point precision to make it easy on the eye. A top brightness of 600 nits also gives it the power to deal comfortably with a range of conditions. The Hisense U6SF supports the major HDR formats, such as Dolby Vision IQ and HDR10+ Adaptive which utlilize their intelligent software alongside sensors in the TV to automatically adjust and optimize the images on the screen so that they best suit the surrounding lighting environment. A dedicated Filmmaker Mode also automatically adjusts the setting so you can enjoy movies just as the creators intended. So, whether its following your favourite sports on a bright sunny afternoon or settling down for an evening with a film classic, the picture will remain balanced, colorful and keep the depth that you need to really lose yourself in the entertainment. Hisense How much room will I need for a MiniLED TV? Another important aspect of choosing a new TV is knowing that it will actually fit into your living space. Thankfully, these days this is a little easier, even though the displays have increased in size. A set like the Hisense U6SF boasts a 65-inch panel, but this is housed in a slim-line unibody design that can be placed close to a wall if you want to sit it on a stand, or you can simply attach it to the wall itself. The built-in speaker system supports Dolby Vision and Atmos surround sound, so there’s no need to attach external speakers, plus the technology that powers the display has the aforementioned anti-reflective and glare-free advantages, plus some clever AI enhancements to ensure that content looks good throughout the day and night. How can AI help improve the performances of a MiniLED TV? Hisense While the term AI can be thrown around quite a lot in the consumer electronics space, sometimes it actually does bring some real-world improvements. Hisense loads up the U6SF with several AI enhancements to make it a truly flexible TV. AI Picture automatically tunes the brightness, contrast and saturation so that it suits the surrounding environment. Paired with the AI light sensor, this ensures that you’ll get peak brightness when the sun is shining, while everything is toned down to make the viewing more comfortable in darker situations. An impressive addition is the AI 4K Upscaler, which uses intelligent software to analyze textures and edges in lower resolution visuals and reconstruct the missing details to bring them up to a 4K equivalence. With this clever feature you can now relax and experience classic content as if it was made today. Sports fans will also appreciate the AI Sports mode and its automatic optimization of settings to create vivid images and pumped up sound to make it seem like you’re in the stadium. This works perfectly with the AI Smooth Motion feature so that all the action avoids any blurs, judders or stutters that could spoil the fun. Is the U6SF TV good for playing games? Hisense Another important role that a modern TV has to play is that of a gaming platform. As consoles and PCs have grown in complexity, the graphical demands they place on displays is more challenging than ever. Traditionally, TVs have lacked the high refresh rates that keep the on-screen action smooth and allow gamers to react instantly to anything thrown at them, often at a frenetic pace. This is where the Hisense U6SF adds another string to its bow, as the panel has a dedicated HDR Game Mode which displays a 144Hz variable refresh rate that can keep up with even the most advanced titles. Thanks to its low-latency motion, the graphics keep clear of stutter and screen tear, while remaining crisp and clear. The Hisense U6SF TV makes it easy to sit back on the sofa and play while still being able to read everything clearly or use split-screen for couch-play with a friend. Its Dolby Atmos surround-sound only adds to the experience, with rich and vibrant soundtracks accompanying your exploits. Upgrade your living room with the Hisense U6SF When you buy a new TV there are plenty of things to consider. Will it last? Can it handle all the latest content? Is it future-proof? How will it fit into my home? Thankfully, the Hisense U6SF has all of these areas covered. The picture will look great in any environment thanks to the AI technology and precise local dimming capabilities. Movies, sports and gaming are equally at home, plus your old content will look even better thanks to the AI 4K upscaler. That’s one less decision to worry about. Upgrade to the Hisense U6SF today! articles.title: Meta’s smartglasses mean any child can be covertly filmed. In the age of AI, how do we tackle that risk?
articles.description: The company argues that it’s for individuals to ensure they don’t ‘actively exploit’ this technology. That won’t keep children safe It took me a while to realise what the man sitting next to me on the train was doing. He was flicking through pictures of a little girl on his phone; zooming in on some, cropping the images. Hardly unusual, of course, except that on closer inspection the pictures were very clearly of the toddler sitting opposite us, playing with her parents. On a crowded train of people mostly staring obliviously at our own phones, a stranger had been covertly photographing that little girl over and over again. And if it hadn’t been for that very visible phone screen giving him away, he wouldn’t have been caught. That encounter was a while ago but my memory was jogged last week listening to a clip of Meta’s VP of wearables, Alex Himel, talk fondly to the BBC about using his new smartglasses to film his daughter singing in a talent contest. They let him capture the memory without having to watch her through a screen, he said, freeing him to be “kind of living in the moment, head up and hands free”. So far, so sweet. But what about the risk of creeps potentially using them to film other people’s daughters covertly, heads up and hands free? Meta’s smartglasses have a tiny flashing warning light on the frame to indicate when the wearer is recording, but the technology is still new enough that many people don’t think to look for it. And in the age of AI, stolen images of children matter. Taken in real life or scraped from the internet , they’re the raw material for generating realistic-looking child abuse material of the most extreme and disturbing kind. (If that sounds like a grim but ultimately fairly victimless crime, the Internet Watch Foundation warned in a recent report that AI-generated material risks fuelling sexual interest in children, normalising violence and increasing the risk of real-life offending.) Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: AI FOMO is a distraction from being a good leader
articles.description: In almost every leadership conversation I have been part of over the last two years, AI comes up within the first ten minutes. Sometimes it is the whole conversation. Executives want to know how to use it, how to talk about it, how to signal that they are not behind on it. There is a palpable anxiety in the room—a fear of being the person who doesn’t get it, who gets left behind, who bets on the wrong tools or moves too slowly while everyone else races ahead. I understand that anxiety. And I want to offer a reframe that I think will be more useful than any AI fluency course. The leaders I see boards choosing right now—the ones rising fastest, the ones being tapped for bigger roles, the ones whose names keep coming up in succession conversations—are almost never the ones who talk most fluently about AI. They are the ones who have spent the last two years doing something much harder and much slower. They have been building trust. Not as a soft skill. Not as a personality trait. As a deliberate, practiced, strategic capability. And it is compounding in ways that no technology adoption ever will. The FOMO is actually costing you Here is what I observe from where I sit as the leader of Egon Zehnder’s FinTech practice. Leaders at every level are devoting enormous energy right now to AI literacy: attending workshops, experimenting with tools, building it into their team workflows, making sure they are seen to be doing all of the above. This is not wrong. AI fluency matters and will continue to matter. But it is acquirable. It can be learned in months. It will be commoditized. And in the succession conversations I am part of, I have never once heard a board say: “The reason we chose her over the other candidates is that she understood AI better.” I have, however, heard boards say things like: “People bring him their real problems.” “Her team would walk through walls for her.” “He is the person in the room everyone wants to be honest with.” “She sees things coming before anyone else because her people tell her the truth.” Those qualities are not acquired at a workshop. They are built over years, in hundreds of small interactions, through habits that most leaders have never been explicitly taught and are not currently developing because they are busy worrying about something else. That is the leadership skills that are in high demand that no one is talking about. What boards are actually evaluating When I am advising boards on CEO succession, the final conversation almost always comes down to one question that is harder to answer than any scorecard item: does this person create an environment where truth travels? Not: do they have AI fluency. But: when things go wrong inside their organization and things always go wrong—do people tell them? Quickly, directly, without softening the edges? That question matters because the higher you rise, the more people manage what they say to you. The instinct to tell the boss what they want to hear is almost universal, and it intensifies as the stakes increase. Leaders who have built genuine trust—the kind where people feel safe enough to be direct—get better information, make faster decisions, and catch problems before they become crises. Leaders who haven’t built it are often the last to know when something is going wrong. This is not a CEO-level concern. A VP who creates that environment outperforms peers who don’t, not because they are smarter or more experienced, but because they are working with reality while everyone else is working with a curated version of it. A director who has earned that kind of trust from their team is already operating at a level above their title. What the leaders who build this actually do differently I have watched leaders develop this quality deliberately, and I have watched others assume they already have it. The gap between those two groups is significant and almost always visible before they are aware of it themselves. The leaders who build genuine trust share four habits that are worth naming—and more importantly, worth practicing. 1. They are curious about people in a way that doesn’t feel transactional. There is a real difference between learning about your colleagues because you genuinely want to understand them and doing it because you know it is good practice to seem interested. People feel this distinction clearly, even when they cannot name it. The leaders who build real trust are interested in the person in front of them independent of what that person can do for them. Try this: before your next one-on-one, set aside the agenda for the first five minutes and ask one question that has nothing to do with work status. Not “how is the project going?” but “what is feeling hard for you right now?” Then listen without redirecting. It will feel unusual at first. That is usually a sign it is working. 2. They say the uncomfortable thing before they are forced to. One of the most trust-building behaviors I observe in senior leaders is the willingness to surface a difficult truth early, when it is still uncomfortable but not yet urgent. This requires a specific kind of confidence: the kind that does not need to be liked in every moment. Leaders who do it consistently become the people their organizations rely on when things get difficult, which is the only time leadership truly matters. Identify one conversation you have been putting off because the timing doesn’t feel quite right. It almost certainly is right. Have it this week, before it becomes a crisis. Name the thing you have been reluctant to say, plainly and with care. The relief on the other side of that conversation, for both of you, will tell you everything about why this habit matters. 3. They know what they don’t know, and they say so out loud. In a moment when AI can produce a confident answer to almost any question in seconds, the leaders who stand out are often the ones willing to say: “I’m not sure. Let me think about that.” Intellectual honesty at the top of a team creates permission for it everywhere. And teams where people are genuinely honest about uncertainty make better decisions than those where they perform certainty they don’t have. For the next two weeks, notice every time you feel the impulse to answer before you have fully thought something through. Sit with that impulse for ten seconds before you speak. This is a small practice with a larger cumulative effect than it sounds. 4. They treat their own reactions as data, not directives. The leaders I have seen build the deepest trust are those who notice when they feel defensive, when feedback lands badly, when they want to dismiss an idea before it has been heard, and who pause before they act on any of it. That pause, small as it sounds, is where the quality of a leader’s judgment is actually formed. After any meeting where you felt reactive, take two minutes and write down what you felt and what triggered it. You do not need to share it with anyone. You just need to see it clearly enough to choose your next move rather than simply react to it. Over time this changes how you show up in difficult conversations in ways that others will notice before you do. A question worth sitting with this week When people walk out of a conversation with you, what do they feel? Do they feel like they told you the truth, or the version of the truth they thought you wanted to hear? Do they leave with more clarity than they arrived with, or less? You can find out. Ask two or three people you work closely with for something specific—not general feedback, but this: “Is there something you have been hesitant to tell me? And is there anything I do that makes it harder to be direct with me?” Ask it in person, not over email. Give them time to answer. Do not explain or defend anything you hear. Just thank them and sit with it. The answers will tell you more about where you actually stand as a leader than any AI tool assessment ever will. AI literacy matters; a really great deal. I am not arguing otherwise. But it is a table stake, not a differentiator—and it is increasingly being treated as a proxy for leadership capability that it was never meant to be. The leaders I see rising are not the ones who have mastered the most tools. They are the ones who have built something that takes years and has no shortcut: the kind of trust that makes people want to tell them the truth. That work was valuable before AI arrived on the scene. It is more valuable now. And the leaders investing in it while everyone else is distracted are the ones I expect to still be rising long after the current moment of AI anxiety has passed. The question is not whether you are keeping up with AI. The question is what you are building while everyone else is busy worrying about it.
